title: Figurative Language
bigQuestion: How can a writer say one thing and mean another, and how do readers know when it is happening?

story.title: Two Men, a Wall and a Question
story.kicker: Robert Frost's poem about repairing a stone wall seems to be about stones, until the reader notices what the stones stand for.
paragraphs: Every spring in northern New England, the ground thaws and the old stone walls between farms tumble a little. Frost heaves the stones. Hunters knock them loose. In 1914 Robert Frost published a poem called Mending Wall about two neighbors who walk the line between their farms each spring, each picking up the fallen stones on his own side and setting them back. For the first several lines, that is all that happens. Stones, hands, a walk.

The poem opens with a line that sounds like a riddle: Something there is that doesn't love a wall. The speaker does not say what the something is. Cold weather, maybe. Or something in nature that dislikes barriers. As he works, he starts to tease his neighbor. There are no cows here to keep in or out, he points out. His apple trees will never cross over and eat the neighbor's pine cones. Why do they need a wall at all?

The neighbor has one answer, and he gives it twice: Good fences make good neighbors. He does not explain. He learned it from his father, and he will not think past it. The speaker watches him carry a stone in each hand and imagines him as an old-stone savage armed, a man from a darker age moving in darkness. That is not a description of a farmer. It is a picture of a mind that has closed.

By the end, a reader realizes the poem was never only about a wall. The wall is a wall, but it is also every barrier people keep up out of habit. The neighbor's saying is a saying, but it is also the way an old idea can keep a person from thinking. And the speaker, who wants the wall gone, still shows up every spring to help rebuild it. The poem does not tell you who is right. It hands you the stones.

This is what figurative language does. It lets a plain thing, a wall, a road, a bird, carry a second weight of meaning without ever announcing it. Frost was a master of it, but the same move happens in speeches, song lyrics, ads and the way your friend says she is drowning in homework. This chapter is about noticing the second weight, naming it and saying what it does.
story.think: The speaker mocks the wall but helps rebuild it every year. What might Frost be suggesting about people who criticize a habit and keep it anyway?

lessons.title: Metaphor and Simile, Closer Up
lessons.mainIdea: A metaphor has two parts, the thing meant and the image used, and the meaning lives in what the two share.
reading: Juliet is the sun. Romeo says so when he sees her at a window: It is the east, and Juliet is the sun. Nobody thinks Juliet is a ball of burning gas. Romeo means that she lights his world, that everything else looks dim next to her, that his day begins when she appears. He has taken one thing, Juliet, and spoken of it as though it were another thing, the sun. That is a *metaphor*. A simile does the same thing but announces the comparison with like or as: her smile was like sunrise.

Every metaphor has two halves. The thing actually being talked about is the *tenor*, here Juliet. The image borrowed to describe it is the *vehicle*, here the sun. The meaning is whatever the two share: brightness, warmth, being the center of things. To read a metaphor, name both halves and then ask what they have in common. Not everything. The sun is also hot enough to burn and impossible to look at. Romeo is not saying that. Context tells you which shared traits count.

Metaphors hide in ordinary speech. Time is money. She has a heart of stone. He shot down my idea. The deadline is looming. We do not notice these because they are worn smooth. But even the worn ones shape thinking. If time is money, then time can be wasted, spent, saved and budgeted, and you will feel that a lazy afternoon is a loss. Notice the vehicle, and you notice the attitude riding inside it.

In your own writing, a fresh metaphor is worth ten adjectives. Instead of the hallway was very crowded and loud, try the hallway was a river at flood. The reader gets crowding, motion, noise and danger in six words. Just keep the vehicle consistent. If the hallway is a river, do not have students marching through it two sentences later. A river does not march.

words.d: a figure of speech that speaks of one thing as if it were another, without like or as
in a metaphor, the actual subject being described
in a metaphor, the image borrowed to describe the subject
a comparison that uses like or as

look.title: Romeo at the Window
look.text: But, soft! what light through yonder window breaks? / It is the east, and Juliet is the sun.
look.cite: William Shakespeare, Romeo and Juliet, Act 2, about 1595
look.prompt: Name the tenor and the vehicle. List two traits of the sun Romeo means and one trait he does not mean, and say how you can tell.

check.q: In Juliet is the sun, what is the vehicle?
choices: Juliet
Romeo
The sun
The window
check.why: The vehicle is the borrowed image, the sun; Juliet is the tenor.

check.q: How does a simile differ from a metaphor?
choices: A simile announces the comparison with like or as
A simile compares only people
A simile is always longer
A simile has no vehicle
check.why: Her smile was like sunrise is a simile; her smile was sunrise is a metaphor.

check.q: What is wrong with the hallway was a river, and students marched through it?
choices: Rivers cannot be in hallways
The metaphor is too short
Marched is a weak verb
The vehicle is inconsistent; a river does not march
check.why: Once the hallway is a river, the action should fit a river: students should flow or be swept.

lessons.title: Extended Metaphor and Conceit
lessons.mainIdea: When a writer keeps one comparison going through a whole poem or passage, every line adds a new point of contact.
reading: Emily Dickinson begins a poem, Hope is the thing with feathers, that perches in the soul. That alone is a metaphor: hope is a bird. But she does not stop. The bird sings a tune without words. It never stops singing. It sings sweetest in the storm. It has kept her warm in the coldest land, and it has never asked her for a crumb. Each line finds one more way a bird and hope are alike. A comparison carried through many lines is an *extended metaphor*.

Reading an extended metaphor means tracking the points of contact. Make two columns: bird on one side, hope on the other. Perches: hope settles in and stays. Sings without words: hope does not need reasons. Sings in the storm: hope is strongest in trouble. Never asks for a crumb: hope costs nothing. When you have the columns, you have the poem. Shakespeare does the same when a character says all the world's a stage and all the men and women merely players, then runs through the seven ages of a life as if they were scenes.

A *conceit* is an extended metaphor that is surprising or far-fetched, joining two things that seem to have nothing in common and making it work anyway. The poet John Donne, writing around 1600, compared two lovers who must part to the two legs of a drawing compass. One leg stays fixed at the center while the other travels in a circle, leaning toward the first, and the fixed leg's steadiness is what makes the circle come out true. A compass is a strange way to talk about love. That strangeness is the point. It forces the reader to think.

Extended metaphors also live outside poetry. A coach calls the season a war and then talks about battles, soldiers and casualties. A politician calls the economy a ship and then speaks of steering, storms and staying the course. Once you spot the vehicle, ask what it makes you feel and what it leaves out. If the economy is a ship, there is one captain. Someone who wants you to trust one leader might like that image very much.

words.d: a single comparison developed over several lines or a whole passage
an extended metaphor that joins two very unlike things in a surprising, clever way
here, a drawing tool with two hinged legs used to make circles

look.title: Hope as a Bird
look.text: Hope is the thing with feathers / That perches in the soul, / And sings the tune without the words, / And never stops at all,
look.cite: Emily Dickinson, poem written about 1861, published 1891
look.prompt: Make the two-column chart for these four lines: what the bird does on one side, what that says about hope on the other. Which line surprised you most?

check.q: What makes a metaphor extended?
choices: It uses like or as
It is carried through several lines, adding new points of contact
It compares two people
It appears in the title
check.why: Dickinson's bird keeps gaining traits across the poem: perching, singing, never asking for a crumb.

check.q: What distinguishes a conceit from an ordinary extended metaphor?
choices: It is shorter
It uses only animals
It joins two things so unlike that the comparison surprises the reader
It always appears in plays
check.why: Donne's lovers as compass legs is far-fetched on purpose; the strangeness makes the reader think.

check.q: Why should a reader be alert when a politician calls the economy a ship?
choices: Because ships are not economic
Because the metaphor is always false
Because it proves the speaker is lying
Because the vehicle implies one captain and may steer the listener toward trusting one leader
check.why: Every vehicle carries hidden attitudes; a ship suggests a single hand on the wheel.

lessons.title: Symbols
lessons.mainIdea: A symbol is a real thing in a text that also stands for an idea, and you know it is a symbol because the text keeps returning to it.
reading: In Mending Wall, the wall is a real wall. Stones fall, the men lift them. But the poem keeps circling back to it, arguing about it, asking what it is for. A thing that is fully itself and also stands for something larger is a *symbol*. The wall stands for the barriers people keep up out of habit. A metaphor says A is B. A symbol just shows you A, over and over, until you feel B standing behind it.

Some symbols are shared by a whole culture. A dove for peace, a red rose for love, a skull for death, a scale for justice, a flag for a nation. You do not need a footnote for these. Others belong to one work only. In Paul Laurence Dunbar's 1896 poem We Wear the Mask, the mask is not a real object. It is the smile Black Americans were forced to wear over pain, the poem says, and the whole poem is the mask being described. The reader learns what it means by reading, not by knowing in advance.

How do you tell a symbol from a mere object? Three tests. Repetition: does the text mention it more than once, especially at important moments? Emphasis: does it appear in the title, the first line or the last? Weight: do characters treat it as more than it is, arguing over it, protecting it, longing for it? A doorknob mentioned once is a doorknob. A locked door the whole story keeps returning to is probably more.

One warning. Students sometimes turn every object into a symbol. The blue curtains mean the author is sad. Usually the blue curtains mean the room had blue curtains. A symbol earns its meaning by the way the text uses it. If you claim something is a symbol, you should be able to point to the repetitions and the moments that gave it weight. If you cannot, let the curtains be curtains.

words.d: a concrete thing in a text that also stands for a larger idea
special stress or importance given to something, such as by placing it first or last
meaning exactly what the words say, with no second meaning

look.title: The Mask
look.text: We wear the mask that grins and lies, / It hides our cheeks and shades our eyes,
look.cite: Paul Laurence Dunbar, We Wear the Mask, 1896
look.prompt: The mask grins, lies, hides and shades. What does it stand for, and who is the we? Which of the three tests for a symbol does the title alone already pass?

check.q: How does a symbol differ from a metaphor?
choices: A symbol uses like or as
A symbol is a real thing in the text that also carries a larger meaning, without saying A is B
A symbol appears only in poetry
A symbol is always an animal
check.why: The wall in Mending Wall is a real wall that also stands for barriers; nobody says the wall is a habit.

check.q: Which is a test for whether an object is a symbol?
choices: Whether the object is blue
Whether the author is famous
Whether the text returns to it at important moments
Whether it is mentioned exactly once
check.why: Repetition, emphasis and weight are the three tests; a thing mentioned once is usually just a thing.

check.q: What does the lesson say about the blue curtains?
choices: They always symbolize sadness
They usually just mean the room had blue curtains, unless the text gives them weight
They are a shared cultural symbol
They are a conceit
check.why: A symbol must earn its meaning through the text's use of it, not through a reader's guess.

lessons.title: Allegory: The Whole Story Stands for Something
lessons.mainIdea: An allegory is a story in which the characters and events line up point by point with a second meaning outside the story.
reading: Imagine a story about a farm where the animals drive out the farmer and run the place themselves. The pigs take charge. They promise equality, then slowly take the farmer's privileges for themselves until nobody can tell pig from man. George Orwell published that story, Animal Farm, in 1945, and every reader knew that the farm was Russia after its revolution and the pigs were the leaders who betrayed it. A story whose characters and events stand, one for one, for something outside the story is an *allegory*.

An allegory is a symbol stretched over a whole narrative. In a symbol, one object carries a second meaning. In an allegory, the whole cast does. John Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress, from 1678, follows a man named Christian who leaves the City of Destruction and walks toward the Celestial City, passing through the Slough of Despond and Vanity Fair. The names give it away. Despond means hopelessness. Vanity means empty pride. The journey is a soul's life, and every stop is a temptation or a trial.

The ancient Greek philosopher Plato told an allegory about prisoners chained in a cave, able to see only shadows on the wall. One escapes, sees the sun and the real world, and returns to tell the others, who do not believe him. The cave is ignorance. The shadows are appearances mistaken for truth. The sun is knowledge. Plato used the story because an argument about knowledge is hard to follow, and a story about a cave is not.

To read an allegory, build the key. Write the story element on one side and its outside meaning on the other: pigs, leaders; cave, ignorance. Then ask what the story lets the writer say that a plain statement could not. Orwell could show betrayal happening step by step. Bunyan could make a life of faith into a road with a map. Allegory turns an idea into something you can watch.

words.d: a story whose characters and events each stand for something outside the story, forming a second meaning
to lose hope; the Slough of Despond in Bunyan's allegory is a swamp of hopelessness
empty pride in appearance or possessions

look.title: Build the Key
look.text: A short film shows a classroom where one student keeps the light switch. When she leaves, students argue about who should hold it. Some want to take turns. A few form a group and lock the switch in a box, then charge the others for light.
look.prompt: Make a two-column key for this allegory: what does the switch stand for, and the students who lock it away? What point does the story make that a speech could not make as well?

check.q: What is the difference between a symbol and an allegory?
choices: A symbol is a single object with a second meaning; an allegory is a whole story whose parts line up with a second meaning
An allegory is shorter
A symbol is always political
An allegory uses like or as
check.why: Allegory is a symbol stretched over an entire narrative, character by character.

check.q: In Plato's cave, what do the shadows represent?
choices: Knowledge
Appearances mistaken for truth
The prisoners' families
The sun
check.why: The prisoners believe the shadows are real, which stands for mistaking appearance for truth.

check.q: Why do writers use allegory instead of stating an idea plainly?
choices: Because allegories are easier to write
Because ideas cannot be stated plainly
Because a story lets readers watch an idea unfold step by step
Because allegories avoid all controversy
check.why: Orwell could show a betrayal happening; a plain statement can only name it.

lessons.title: Three Kinds of Irony
lessons.mainIdea: Irony is a gap between what is said or expected and what is true, and it comes in verbal, situational and dramatic forms.
reading: It is pouring rain, and your friend says, Great weather for a picnic. She means the opposite of what she says, and she expects you to know it. That is *verbal irony*, saying one thing to mean another. When it is meant to sting, it is sarcasm. Verbal irony works only if the listener catches the gap. Tone of voice, context and a shared sense of how things are all help. In writing, where there is no tone of voice, the context has to do the whole job.

*Situational irony* is a gap between what is expected and what happens. A fire station burns down. A lifeguard drowns. In O. Henry's 1905 story The Gift of the Magi, a young wife sells her long hair to buy a chain for her husband's watch. He, the same day, sells the watch to buy combs for her hair. Each gift is now useless, and each is perfect. Nobody said the opposite of what they meant; the situation itself turned inside out.

*Dramatic irony* is a gap between what a character knows and what the audience knows. At the end of Romeo and Juliet, Romeo finds Juliet in the tomb and believes she is dead. The audience knows she has only taken a sleeping potion and will wake in minutes. We want to shout at him. That helplessness, watching a character act on a mistake we can see and he cannot, is the feeling dramatic irony creates. Horror films use it constantly: the audience knows what is behind the door.

To name the irony in a text, first find the gap. Between words and meaning: verbal. Between expectation and outcome: situational. Between a character's knowledge and the audience's: dramatic. Then ask what the gap does. Verbal irony often makes a speaker sound sharp or amused. Situational irony makes a story feel like fate or a joke. Dramatic irony makes an audience tense or sad. Irony is never just decoration. It always shifts how the reader feels.

words.d: saying one thing while meaning the opposite, expecting the listener to notice
a gap between what is expected to happen and what actually happens
a gap between what a character knows and what the audience knows
verbal irony meant to mock or wound

look.title: Sort the Three
look.text: A. A character hides in the one closet the audience just saw the villain enter. B. A student who wrote an essay against cell phones in class wins a phone as the prize. C. Someone spills soup on her shirt and says, Smooth move.
look.prompt: Label each situation verbal, situational or dramatic irony and explain the gap in each. Which one would make you laugh, and which would make you tense?

check.q: Which is an example of situational irony?
choices: A character says nice job after a teammate drops the ball
The audience knows the letter never arrived, but the hero does not
A fire station burns down
A poem compares hope to a bird
check.why: A fire station is expected to prevent fires; its burning is a gap between expectation and outcome.

check.q: What creates dramatic irony in the tomb scene of Romeo and Juliet?
choices: Romeo says the opposite of what he means
The audience knows Juliet is alive, and Romeo does not
Juliet expected Romeo and he did not come
The tomb is a symbol
check.why: The gap is between the character's knowledge and the audience's.

check.q: Why does verbal irony in writing depend so heavily on context?
choices: Because written irony is illegal in essays
Because writers never use sarcasm
Because irony only works in poems
Because there is no tone of voice on the page to signal the gap
check.why: In speech, tone shows the gap; in writing, the surrounding words must do that work.

lessons.title: Paradox and Oxymoron
lessons.mainIdea: A paradox seems to contradict itself but holds a truth, and an oxymoron packs that contradiction into two words.
reading: In Hamlet, the prince says, I must be cruel only to be kind. On its face that makes no sense. Cruelty is the opposite of kindness. But Hamlet means that harsh words now may save his mother from a worse fate later, the way a doctor may hurt you to heal you. A statement that seems to contradict itself and yet turns out to be true is a *paradox*. The reader's job is to find the sense hidden inside the contradiction.

Paradoxes appear wherever a writer wants to stop you cold. The witches in Macbeth chant, Fair is foul, and foul is fair, and the whole play proves them right: what looks good turns out evil, and evil wears a fair face. Everyday speech has them too. Less is more. You have to spend money to make money. The only constant is change. Each one forces you to pause and work out how both halves can hold.

An *oxymoron* is a paradox shrunk to a phrase, usually two words that fight each other. Deafening silence. Jumbo shrimp. Bittersweet. Living dead. Juliet says parting is such sweet sorrow, and the sweet and the sorrow are both true: it hurts to leave, and it is sweet because she will see him again. The oxymoron does in two words what a paragraph of explanation might do, and it does it with a jolt.

When you meet a paradox or an oxymoron, do not dismiss it as nonsense. Ask under what conditions both halves can be true. Deafening silence: silence so complete that it feels like a pressure on the ears. Cruel to be kind: cruel now, kind in the long run. The figure is a small puzzle, and solving it is often the moment the writer's meaning opens up. If it cannot be solved, then the writer may simply have made an error, but that is rare in good writing.

words.d: a statement that seems to contradict itself but contains a truth
a figure of speech that joins two contradictory words, such as deafening silence
to state the opposite of something; to be in conflict with it

look.title: Hamlet's Puzzle
look.text: I must be cruel, only to be kind.
look.prompt: Under what conditions can cruelty and kindness both be true at once? Give an example from ordinary life, such as a coach, a parent or a doctor, that fits the line.

check.q: What is a paradox?
choices: A statement that seems self-contradictory but holds a truth
A comparison using like or as
A word that means its opposite
A story with a hidden meaning
check.why: Cruel to be kind seems impossible until you see cruelty now can produce kindness later.

check.q: Which phrase is an oxymoron?
choices: Time is money
Deafening silence
Good fences make good neighbors
Juliet is the sun
check.why: Deafening and silence contradict each other in a single two-word phrase.

check.q: What should a reader do when a statement seems to contradict itself?
choices: Assume the writer made an error
Skip it as decoration
Ask under what conditions both halves could be true
Rewrite it as a simile
check.why: Solving the small puzzle is usually the moment the writer's meaning opens.

lessons.title: Allusion and How to Look One Up
lessons.mainIdea: An allusion borrows a famous story in a few words, and a reader who does not know the story can find it in a minute.
reading: In 1858, Abraham Lincoln opened a speech about slavery with the words, A house divided against itself cannot stand. He did not invent the line. It comes from the Gospel of Mark, and his listeners knew it. By borrowing it, Lincoln made the nation into a house and let the Bible's authority stand behind his warning without arguing for it. A brief reference to a well-known story, person, place or text is an *allusion*. It works by trust: the writer trusts you to know the reference.

Allusions come from a few big sources. Biblical: a good Samaritan is a stranger who helps; a David against a Goliath is a small fighter against a giant; a prodigal son is a wanderer who comes home. Classical, from Greek and Roman myth: an Achilles heel is one fatal weakness; a Pandora's box is a source of troubles better left shut; a Trojan horse is a gift hiding an attack; a task like Sisyphus's never ends. Historical: to meet your Waterloo is to suffer your final defeat, after the battle where Napoleon lost in 1815. Literary: a Scrooge is a miser, from Dickens.

The problem is that nobody knows every story, and writers do not stop to explain. So learn to look one up fast. Take the odd phrase, the name or the place you do not recognize, and search it with the word meaning or origin. Read a source you trust, an encyclopedia or a dictionary of allusions, not the first comment thread. Then go back to the sentence and ask what the story adds. Usually it adds a whole plot in three words.

Allusions also appear in songs, films and titles. A team called the Titans alludes to giants of Greek myth. A headline about a modern Trojan horse is warning about a hidden threat. Once you start noticing, you will find that much of what you read is quietly quoting something older. Knowing the source is like getting the joke that everyone else was already laughing at.

words.d: a brief reference to a well-known story, person, place or text that the reader is expected to recognize
a single weak spot in someone otherwise strong, from the Greek hero who could be wounded only in the heel
a final, crushing defeat, from the 1815 battle Napoleon lost

look.title: Lincoln Borrows a Line
look.text: A house divided against itself cannot stand.
look.cite: Abraham Lincoln, speech at Springfield, Illinois, June 16, 1858, quoting the Gospel of Mark
look.prompt: What is the house in Lincoln's speech, and what divides it? Why might a borrowed line carry more force than an original one in this case?

check.q: What is an allusion?
choices: A brief reference to a well-known story or text the reader is expected to know
A statement that contradicts itself
A comparison using like or as
A softer word for a harsh thing
check.why: Lincoln's house divided borrowed a Bible verse his audience recognized.

check.q: What does it mean to call a problem someone's Achilles heel?
choices: Their greatest strength
A gift hiding an attack
A source of endless troubles
Their one fatal weakness
check.why: Achilles could be wounded only in the heel, so the phrase names a single weak spot.

check.q: What is the best way to look up an unfamiliar allusion?
choices: Ask a friend to guess
Search the phrase with meaning or origin and read a trusted reference
Skip it, since allusions rarely matter
Look it up in a thesaurus
check.why: A quick search of the phrase plus a reliable source recovers the story in a minute.

lessons.title: Euphemism: The Softer Word
lessons.mainIdea: A euphemism replaces a blunt word with a gentler one, and readers should ask whether it is kindness or a way to hide the truth.
reading: Nobody at a funeral says the person died. They say she passed away, she is gone, we lost her. A company does not fire two hundred workers; it lets them go, or downsizes, or restructures. A used car is pre-owned. A lie is a misstatement. Each of these is a *euphemism*, a mild or indirect word put in place of one that is harsh, embarrassing or frightening. The word comes from Greek parts meaning good speech.

Some euphemisms are simple kindness. Passed away lets a grieving family avoid a blunt word in a hard hour. Restroom spares everyone a description. Nobody is fooled and nobody is harmed. But other euphemisms are built to fool. When a military report says collateral damage, it means civilians were killed. When a budget speaks of revenue enhancements, it means taxes went up. The soft word is there to keep you from feeling what the hard word would make you feel.

The test is simple. Translate the euphemism into the plainest word you can, and ask whether the writer wanted you to. If the plain word is died and the setting is a funeral, the euphemism is doing gentle work. If the plain word is killed and the setting is a report meant to reassure the public, the euphemism is doing dishonest work. Notice, too, that euphemisms tend to be longer and vaguer than the words they replace. Extra syllables are often extra distance from the truth.

As a writer, use euphemism on purpose and rarely. In a note to a grieving friend, passed away is right. In an analysis of a company's decision, write that it fired workers, because that is what happened. And when you catch a euphemism in a speech, an ad or a news release, name it in your writing. Saying that a speaker called layoffs a restructuring is itself a sharp piece of analysis.

words.d: a mild or indirect word used in place of a harsh, blunt or embarrassing one
a military euphemism for civilians killed or property destroyed unintentionally
plain and direct, without softening

look.title: Plain Word, Soft Word
look.prompt: Each pair shows a plain word and then its euphemism. What pattern do you see in the counts, and why might a softer word tend to be a longer one?

check.q: What is a euphemism?
choices: A word that contradicts itself
A mild or indirect word used in place of a harsh one
A reference to a famous story
A comparison between two unlike things
check.why: Passed away for died and let go for fired are euphemisms.

check.q: When is a euphemism most likely dishonest, according to the lesson?
choices: When it is used at a funeral
When it is shorter than the plain word
When it keeps the public from feeling what the plain word would reveal
When it comes from Greek
check.why: Collateral damage for civilian deaths exists to blunt the reader's reaction to a hard fact.

check.q: What is the lesson's test for judging a euphemism?
choices: Count its letters
Check whether it appears in a dictionary
Ask whether it rhymes with the plain word
Translate it into the plainest word and ask whether the writer wanted you to
check.why: If the writer would rather you not translate it, the euphemism is hiding something.

lessons.title: Reading a Figure in Its Context
lessons.mainIdea: The same figure of speech can mean different things in different passages, so always read it against the sentences around it.
reading: Take the phrase cold as ice. In one story: her hands were cold as ice after an hour in the snow. That is a simile about temperature, nearly literal. In another: her voice was cold as ice when she told him to leave. Now it means unfriendly, controlled, without warmth. Same words, different meaning, and only the context tells you which. A figure of speech is never a fixed code. It is a suggestion that the surrounding sentences complete.

Here is a harder case. A character says, Well, that went well. If the previous paragraph showed a smooth meeting, the sentence is literal. If it showed a meeting that ended with someone storming out, it is verbal irony. Nothing in the sentence itself changes. Readers who miss the irony are not bad readers of the sentence. They are readers who did not carry the previous paragraph with them. Figures of speech make you hold more of the text in your head at once.

Sometimes a whole poem has to be read before its central figure settles. In Frost's Mending Wall, the line Good fences make good neighbors sounds wise the first time the neighbor says it. By the second time, after the speaker has mocked it and imagined the neighbor moving in darkness, the same words sound stubborn and unexamined. The line did not change. The context around it did, and the reader's understanding changed with it.

So when you interpret a figure, do three things. Read the sentence and identify the figure. Read the surrounding paragraph, and if needed the whole passage, to see what it is pointing at. Then state the meaning in plain words, and be ready to say which context clues told you. Cold voice: the sentence says voice, not hands, and she is telling him to leave. That is evidence. An interpretation without evidence is just a guess.

words.d: an expression that means something other than its literal words, such as a metaphor or irony
to explain the meaning of something, especially something not stated directly
the words, sentences and situation surrounding a word or phrase

look.title: Same Words, Two Rooms
look.text: 1. After the championship, the captain lifted the trophy and said, We climbed the mountain. 2. After the third loss in a row, the captain looked at the empty stands and said, We climbed the mountain.
look.prompt: What does the metaphor mean in the first case? What does it mean in the second, and what kind of figure has it become? Point to the exact context words that changed it.

check.q: Why can cold as ice mean two different things?
choices: Because ice has two temperatures
Because the surrounding context decides whether it is about temperature or feeling
Because it is an oxymoron
Because one use is a simile and the other a metaphor
check.why: Hands after an hour in the snow is temperature; a voice telling someone to leave is unfriendliness.

check.q: What does a reader need to catch the irony in that went well?
choices: A dictionary
Knowledge of the Greek root
The previous paragraph showing how the meeting actually went
The character's name
check.why: The sentence is identical either way; only the earlier events reveal the gap.

check.q: How does the meaning of Good fences make good neighbors change in Mending Wall?
choices: It changes from a saying to a literal instruction
The neighbor changes the words the second time
It goes from an insult to praise
It sounds wise at first and stubborn after the speaker's mockery and the image of darkness
check.why: The words stay the same; the surrounding lines shift how the reader hears them.

lessons.title: What a Figure Does to Tone
lessons.mainIdea: Figurative language changes not only what a sentence means but how it feels, and naming that feeling is the heart of analysis.
reading: Read two versions. First: the city was crowded and noisy that night. Second: the city was a hive that night, humming and swarming. Both report the same facts. The second makes you feel something the first does not. A hive is busy, crowded and alive, but also organized and a little dangerous, with the possibility of stings. The metaphor did not add information. It added *tone*, the writer's attitude toward the subject, and it added mood, the feeling produced in the reader.

Different figures push tone in different directions. Metaphor and simile can make a subject grand or small depending on the vehicle: the senator was a lion, the senator was a wet hen. Irony makes a speaker sound amused, bitter or superior. Euphemism softens and, if overused, makes a writer sound evasive. Allusion can make a passage feel learned or solemn, as Lincoln's Bible verse did. Oxymoron and paradox make a reader stop and think, which slows the pace and feels serious.

So when you write about a text, do not stop at the label. The author uses a metaphor is a beginning, not an analysis. Go on: the metaphor compares the city to a hive, and the vehicle suggests both energy and danger, so the passage feels exciting and slightly threatening at once. Three moves: name the figure, unpack the vehicle, state the effect on tone. Every good paragraph about figurative language has all three.

Try it on Frost. When the speaker sees his neighbor as an old-stone savage armed, the figure is a metaphor. The vehicle is a prehistoric man carrying weapons. The effect is to make the neighbor seem not evil but stuck in the dark, and to make the speaker sound a little superior, which the poem may or may not approve of. That last uncertainty is fine. Tone is often mixed, and saying so honestly is stronger than forcing one answer.

words.d: the writer's attitude toward the subject, shown through word choice and figures of speech
the feeling a passage creates in the reader
avoiding a direct answer; slippery

look.title: Two Descriptions of One Storm
look.text: A. The storm arrived at six and dropped two inches of rain in an hour. B. The storm came in like an army, drumming on the roofs and flinging the trees around by the hair.
look.prompt: Which version has tone, and what is it? Name the figures in B, unpack one vehicle and state its effect in a single sentence using the three moves.

check.q: What does the hive metaphor add to the sentence about the city?
choices: More facts about the city
A feeling of energy and slight danger
A definition of the word city
A historical allusion
check.why: Both versions report the same facts; the hive adds attitude and mood.

check.q: What are the three moves in analyzing a figure of speech?
choices: Name the figure, unpack the vehicle, state the effect on tone
Find the root, prefix and suffix
Count the syllables, lines and stanzas
Quote it, translate it, memorize it
check.why: The label alone is only a beginning; the analysis lives in the vehicle and the effect.

check.q: What does the lesson say about a tone that seems mixed?
choices: Mixed tone means the writer failed
Choose one tone and ignore the rest
Saying honestly that the tone is mixed is stronger than forcing one answer
Mixed tone only occurs in poetry
check.why: Frost's speaker sounds both perceptive and superior; a careful reader can say both.

lessons.title: Using Figures in Your Own Writing
lessons.mainIdea: A fresh, consistent figure strengthens your writing, while a cliché or a mixed metaphor weakens it.
reading: A student writes: At the end of the day, the team hit the ground running and gave 110 percent. Every phrase is a figure of speech, and every one is dead. A *cliché* is a figure so overused that it no longer makes a picture. The reader slides over it. Nobody sees a ground or a runner. Compare: the team came out like it had been waiting behind a door all week. The reader sees the door. Freshness is the difference between a figure that works and one that fills space.

The second danger is the *mixed metaphor*, two vehicles that cannot share a sentence. We will iron out the bottlenecks. You cannot iron a bottle. The ship of state has hit a bump in the road. Ships do not travel roads. Mixed metaphors happen when a writer uses figures without seeing them. The cure is to see them. Before you keep a metaphor, picture it. If the picture is absurd, change one half.

Figures belong in analysis too, in moderation. Writing that Frost's speaker circles the wall like a lawyer circling a witness makes a point vividly. But an analytical essay should mostly explain figures, not pile up its own. One well-placed comparison in an introduction or conclusion is enough. Let the text you are analyzing supply the poetry, and let your sentences supply the clarity.

A short practice. Take a plain sentence from your last essay. Find its most important noun. Ask what it is like, and reject the first two answers, since they will be the clichés. Take the third, check that the vehicle fits, and rewrite. Then read the new sentence aloud. If you can see the picture and it sounds like you, keep it. If it sounds like a greeting card, you have found a cliché, and you already know what to do.

words.d: a figure of speech so overused that it no longer creates a picture
two incompatible vehicles combined in one figure, such as ironing out a bottleneck
producing a clear, strong picture in the mind

look.title: Fix the Sentence
look.text: Draft: When the rubber meets the road, our student council will grab the bull by the horns and sail through the storm to reach new heights.
look.prompt: Count the figures. Which are clichés, and where do the vehicles collide? Rewrite the sentence with one fresh, consistent figure and no more.

check.q: Why does a cliché weaken writing?
choices: Because it is grammatically wrong
Because it is too long
Because it is so familiar that it no longer makes a picture
Because it is always a simile
check.why: Readers slide over hit the ground running without seeing anything.

check.q: Which sentence contains a mixed metaphor?
choices: The hallway was a river at flood, sweeping us toward the doors.
Her voice was cold as ice.
The plan is a house of cards.
We will iron out the bottlenecks in the plan.
check.why: Ironing and bottlenecks are two vehicles that cannot combine; the others keep one picture.

check.q: What does the lesson advise about figures in an analytical essay?
choices: Use one well-placed figure and let the text supply the poetry
Avoid figures entirely
Use a figure in every paragraph
Use only similes, never metaphors
check.why: The essay's job is to explain the text's figures clearly, not to compete with them.

review.q: In Mending Wall, what does the wall come to stand for beyond itself?
choices: The speaker's apple orchard
Barriers people keep up out of habit
The cold New England weather
The neighbor's father
review.why: The poem returns to the wall until it carries the weight of every barrier maintained without thought.

review.q: In the metaphor Juliet is the sun, Juliet is the
choices: Vehicle
Simile
Tenor
Symbol
review.why: The tenor is the actual subject; the sun is the borrowed vehicle.

choices: An extended metaphor that joins two very unlike things in a surprising way
A gentle word used in place of a harsh one
A phrase of two contradictory words
A reference to a famous story
review.why: Donne's lovers as compass legs is the classic example.

review.q: A lifeguard drowns. What kind of irony is this?
choices: Verbal
Dramatic
Sarcasm
Situational
review.why: The outcome is the opposite of what the situation leads us to expect.

choices: Time is money
Sweet sorrow
A house divided
Cold as ice
review.why: Sweet and sorrow contradict each other in one short phrase.

review.q: Calling a hidden threat a Trojan horse is an example of
choices: Euphemism
Paradox
Allusion
Mixed metaphor
review.why: It refers to the Greek story of the gift that concealed soldiers.

choices: Collateral damage for civilian deaths
Deafening silence
The ship of state
An Achilles heel
review.why: Collateral damage softens the fact of civilians killed.

review.q: Which is the strongest analysis of a figure of speech?
choices: The author uses a metaphor here.
The author compares the city to a hive.
The author uses figurative language to make the passage interesting.
The hive metaphor suggests energy and danger, giving the passage an excited, uneasy tone.
review.why: It names the figure, unpacks the vehicle and states the effect on tone.
